clue.text: Fredericks, say, involved in a run out from gully

indicators.note: something involved in a matter is caught up inside it, so one piece sits within the others

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a run
Roy Fredericks was a West Indies opening batsman; 'say' marks him as an example of someone called this
O stands for out, as in a duck or a dismissal

explanation.surface: A cricketer called Fredericks is run out after the ball is fielded in the gully.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket words all pull toward the fielding position, but gully is the definition in its landscape sense: a steep-sided water channel.
explanation.definitionFit: An arroyo is a dry stream bed or steep-sided watercourse in arid country, which is a kind of gully.

clue.text: Lap dancer close to lascivious tourist

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is used

blocks.note: the last letter of lascivious
a day tripper is a tourist on a short outing

explanation.surface: A lap dancer gets up close to a leering holidaymaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' reads as nearness in the surface, but here it means the closing letter of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A lap dancer is one kind of erotic performer who removes clothing, so the more general term fits as an example.

clue.text: Spot politician entering large building

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: MP is a Member of Parliament
a pile is a large, imposing building, such as a stately home

explanation.surface: Someone spots a politician going into a grand building.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot is a small skin blemish, the everyday synonym for a pimple.

clue.text: Odd having left in choke

indicators.note: to have something is to hold it, so the first word holds the second within it

blocks.note: odd and strange are synonyms
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Something strange happens when someone departs while choking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left in' looks like a phrase on its own, but 'having' does the work of putting the left letter inside the odd word, and 'in' just joins to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To strangle someone is to choke them by squeezing the throat, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Parliamentary leader, oldest one in church

indicators.note: one thing in another sits within it, so the single letter goes inside the place of worship

blocks.note: the oldest is the first to have come along
the Roman numeral for one
a minster is a large church, as at York

explanation.surface: The longest-serving MP is spotted at a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scottish and Welsh parliaments are each led by a First Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: First Minister is the title of the head of government in the devolved Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish administrations.

clue.text: Monopoly has started here since it first came out

blocks.note: first meaning: every game of Monopoly begins on the corner square marked GO
second meaning: an idiom for right from the very beginning

explanation.surface: A history of the board game Monopoly, popular ever since its launch.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is literal: players set off from the square labelled GO.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means from the very start, which is how long something has been true if true since it first appeared.

clue.text: Sharing similar problems, like the three with Montmorency?

blocks.note: first meaning: an idiom for being in the same difficult situation as others
second meaning: literally, Jerome K. Jerome's Three Men in a Boat travel with their dog Montmorency

explanation.surface: A comparison between people in trouble and the heroes of a comic Victorian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Montmorency is the fox terrier in Jerome K. Jerome's Three Men in a Boat; the question mark flags the literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes people facing the same difficulties, and the novel's three men literally share one rowing boat.

clue.text: Ran over short updated article being circulated

indicators.note: something short is cut off before its end, so the word loses its last letter
letters being circulated are passed around and rearranged into a new order

blocks.note: the word without its final D
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone summarises a news article that has been revised and passed round the office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran over' suggests a traffic accident, but it means went over again in summary.
explanation.definitionFit: To recapitulate is to summarise the main points again, which is what running over a talk or argument means.

clue.text: Settler on island wearing revolver

indicators.note: whoever is wearing something has it around them, so the gun goes around the other letters

blocks.note: taken as written
IS is a standard abbreviation for island
a Colt is a famous make of revolver

explanation.surface: A frontier settler on an island carries a revolver.
explanation.definitionFit: A colonist is someone who settles in a new territory, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Location, we hear, for flatfish

indicators.note: what we hear is a spoken sound, so the word is chosen by how it is pronounced

blocks.note: a location is a place

explanation.surface: A query about where to find a particular flatfish.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaice is a common European flatfish with orange spots, eaten widely in Britain.

clue.text: The sea prom's polluted air

indicators.note: polluted things are spoiled and mixed up, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters used as fodder

explanation.surface: A complaint that the seafront promenade has dirty air.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining the fodder to its indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: The atmosphere is the envelope of gases around the earth, the air we breathe.

clue.text: Good mimic may get one to stare open-mouthed

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
to ape is to mimic

explanation.surface: A talented impressionist leaves the audience gawping in amazement.
explanation.definitionFit: To gape is to stare in wonder with the mouth wide open, an exact match for the phrase.

clue.text: Fun meant Internet surfing?

indicators.note: surfing tumbles about on waves, suggesting the letters are churned into a new order

blocks.note: the letters used as fodder

explanation.surface: A question whether browsing the web was intended as amusement.
explanation.definitionFit: Entertainment is amusement or enjoyment, so fun is a direct synonym.

clue.text: United shot over during tie

indicators.note: turned over means flipped round, so the word is read backwards
something happening during another event falls within it, so it sits inside

blocks.note: a shot is a go, an attempt
to tether is to tie up an animal

explanation.surface: A football report: a United shot flies over the bar during a cup tie.
explanation.walkthrough: United and tie both sound like football, but United is the definition and tie is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: People who are together are united, joined as one, so the adjective fits.

clue.text: Restricted access here in sporting arena hosting ordinary match

indicators.note: sporting can mean playing about, so the letters frolic into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level
colours that match go together

explanation.surface: Fans are kept out of part of a stadium staging an everyday fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' means go with, not a game, despite the sporting surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-go area is a district where entry is barred or dangerous, a place of restricted access.

clue.text: Bell sounding? I must leave

indicators.note: a letter that must leave is taken out of the word

blocks.note: a bell that is going is ringing out
the letter removed

explanation.surface: Someone hears a bell ring and announces it is time to depart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I must leave' reads like a person excusing themselves; it is the instruction to remove the I.
explanation.definitionFit: A gong is a metal disc struck to sound a signal, a kind of bell.

clue.text: Fun galore I fancy in a Spanish resort

indicators.note: fancy describes something elaborate and reworked, so the letters take an ornate new order

blocks.note: the letters used as fodder

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker expects plenty of fun at a resort in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Fuengirola is a beach resort town on the Costa del Sol in southern Spain.

clue.text: Litter removed by bank

blocks.note: far removed means distant
a bank is a row, as of keys or lights

explanation.surface: Rubbish is cleared away beside a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: Litter is not rubbish but a brood of young animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A farrow is a litter of piglets, a sow's young born together.

clue.text: Viking leader's name for an undergarment

blocks.note: Rollo was the Viking chief who founded the duchy of Normandy
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A historical oddity: what a Viking chief called his underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is possessive in the surface but just joins Rollo to the name letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll-on is an elasticated girdle pulled on over the hips, a woman's foundation garment.

clue.text: Journalist travelled back to collect it

indicators.note: going back means heading the opposite way, so the word is read from its end
to collect something is to gather it in, so the word holds the other within it

blocks.note: rode is a past tense of travel by horse or vehicle
taken as written

explanation.surface: A reporter goes back somewhere to pick something up.
explanation.definitionFit: An editor is a senior journalist who prepares and oversees what a newspaper publishes.

clue.text: Referring to a head describing one who's learning with little effort

indicators.note: to describe can mean to draw around, so these letters go around the other piece

blocks.note: on means referring to, and a pate is a head
L is the learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A puzzling description of a learner who gets things without trying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' is used in its geometric sense of drawing a line around something.
explanation.definitionFit: Handed something on a plate means given it without having to work for it, an idiom for little effort.

clue.text: Last drink of person going from one saloon to another?

definitions.text: Last drink of person going from one saloon to another?

blocks.clueFragment: Last drink of person going from one saloon to another?
blocks.note: surface reading: a pub crawler's final drink before moving to the next bar
setter's reading: a saloon is also a car, so the drinker is about to drive, and a final drink is taken before the journey

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a saloon is a car with a closed body as well as a bar, so one saloon to another is from the pub to the car.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a final drink taken just before setting off on a journey home.
